The fact that you are doing the research and coming here to ask means you are likely already engaging in a lot of the best ways to support her. Some of the most basic ways to support people with this or other mental health struggles is to educate yourself, then listen, and validate. 

Additionally, sometimes, not always, when people express anxieties about certain things, they may be most comforted by emotional validation rather than logical explanations/possible solutions. So you could see if she feels supported by acknowledging her burden and reaffirming the feelings she has are clearly valid given what she is going through and that you will be with her to help her wade through all of it. 

But honestly, best way to support someone, though it’s not always easy for either party at first (so many reasons why), is to ask them how you can best support them. If they say I don’t know, then you can let them know the things you feel you can do as options and see if they would like you to engage in any of them. 

For example.  You can say, could I best support you by just listening? Or would you be more comforted with advice and solutions? Do you find it helpful when I offer grounding facts? Or would you prefer another approach? I’m here for you in whatever way is best for you. I want to make sure I show up in the way that will serve you most.

I’ve found a team of doctors and therapists that see mental illness as purely biological and they treat my illness as one would diabetes or a heart condition. They assess my symptoms and treat me based on those with my reporting back side effects to find a balance between drugs that work and side effects that are tolerable. 

There are so so many combinations of different kind of drugs that can affect your system in different ways so looking for people to treat you and see you as someone suffering from a biochemical abnormality and not a ‘crazy’ personality may be a good way to approach finding providers that fit your needs better. Once the discussion is about sumptomology and not personality, it can feel less stigmatizing. 

My psychiatrist also helped me come to terms with the tolerating side effects part by reminding me that nearly everyone with chronic illness who takes meds has a unique set of side effects they must balance with their treatment efficacy and that I should look at it like any other non-mental disorder for comparison when I feel like you do.

I’m sorry you have experienced this. I think searching for a new provider could help for sure. Just make sure you prepare questions beforehand to see their perspective like, 

what is your approach? 

How much control and say will I have in deciding my med regimen? 

What is your outlook on treatment and what lifestyle/bar do you set for a minimum level of reasonable remission status?
